title: Video-delivered group exercise for knee osteoarthritis in a rural physiotherapy service
subtitle: Mixed-methods evaluation of outcomes and acceptability
statement: A regional hospital physiotherapy service has offered a six-week group exercise programme for knee osteoarthritis by video since March 2026; 64 people have started and 49 completed it. Before the hospital decides whether to keep the programme and whether to offer it instead of the in-person class for some patients, the service needs to know how participants' knee symptoms and function change and who finds video delivery workable, particularly older people, people with poor internet and people whose first language is not English.
whoAffected: Adults with knee osteoarthritis waiting for physiotherapy in a large rural catchment, their families who help with devices, and the physiotherapists who run the groups.
whatHurts: Five-month waits and long journeys delay exercise therapy; people who cannot manage video may be left with no workable option if the in-person class is reduced.
currentPractice: An in-person six-week class at the hospital and, since March, the same content by video; KOOS-12, the chair stand test and attendance are recorded routinely.
whyNow: The hospital will decide on the programme's future in 2027, and early reports of drop-out after connection problems suggest that access may be unequal.
constraints: No funding beyond staff time. The video programme cannot be withheld from anyone who wants it. Interviews must be done by a physiotherapist who does not run the participant's own group. Data collection must finish by June 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Every person with knee osteoarthritis gets exercise therapy they can attend, in a format that works for them, with outcomes at least as good as the in-person class.
summary: Problem framed as a mixed-methods evaluation of a video exercise programme's outcomes and acceptability.
